searched: 2026-10-12. PubMed (NCBI E-utilities esearch/esummary/efetch; every abstract below was retrieved and read from the PubMed record at the listed PMID). DOIs taken from the PubMed record. Full texts were not read; numbers come from abstracts only.
scope_note: Lab changes in mechanics are not injury reduction. Each 'result' states the outcome actually measured. Only Chan 2018 (impact-feedback RCT) shows injury reduction in a trial; Doyle 2022 notes two trials with reduced 1-year injury incidence. Ranges/thresholds are not given here.

suggestions.cue: Increase step rate 5-10% (metronome or watch cadence alert); 'quicker, shorter steps', 'land with the foot closer under your hips'.

evidence.citation: Heiderscheit BC, Chumanov ES, Michalski MP, Wille CM, Ryan MB 2011. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 43(2):296-302
evidence.population: 45 healthy recreational runners, treadmill, step rate preferred, +/-5%, +/-10%
evidence.result: Less knee energy absorption at +5% and +10% step rate; less hip energy absorption at +10% only. Step length, COM vertical excursion, braking impulse and peak knee flexion decreased as step rate increased. At +10%: peak hip adduction angle and hip adduction and internal rotation moments decreased. -10% step rate increased energy absorption at all joints.

evidence.citation: Lenhart RL, Thelen DG, Wille CM, Chumanov ES, Heiderscheit BC 2014. Increasing running step rate reduces patellofemoral joint forces. Med Sci Sports Exerc 46(3):557-64
evidence.population: 30 healthy adults, instrumented treadmill, 90/100/110% preferred step rate
evidence.result: 110% step rate reduced peak patellofemoral joint force by 14%; hip, knee, ankle extensor and hip abductor forces reduced in midstance; reduced peak stance knee flexion was the main predictor of the PFJ load reduction.

evidence.citation: Willy RW, Buchenic L, Rogacki K, Ackerman J, Schmidt A, Willson JD 2016. In-field gait retraining and mobile monitoring to address running biomechanics associated with tibial stress fracture. Scand J Med Sci Sports 26(2):197-205
evidence.population: 30 healthy runners with high impact forces (retraining vs control)
evidence.result: Cued +7.5% step rate via wireless accelerometer, 8 in-field sessions. Step rate +8.6%; instantaneous vertical load rate -17.9%; average vertical load rate -18.9%; peak hip adduction reduced 2.9 deg (SD 4.2); eccentric knee work per stance -26.9%. Changes maintained at 30 days. No injury outcome.

evidence.citation: Doyle E, Doyle TLA, Bonacci J, Fuller JT 2022. The Effectiveness of Gait Retraining on Running Kinematics, Kinetics, Performance, Pain, and Injury in Distance Runners: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 52(4):192-206
evidence.population: 19 RCTs, 673 participants
evidence.result: Moderate-certainty: step rate retraining increased step rate (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.63-1.44) and reduced average vertical loading rate (SMD -0.57, -1.05 to -0.09). Low-certainty: non-rearfoot strike retraining increased knee flexion at initial contact (SMD 0.74, 0.11-1.37), no change in running economy. Insufficient trials on pain; two trials showed reduced 1-year injury incidence.

evidence.citation: Luedke LE, Heiderscheit BC, Williams DS, Rauh MJ 2016. Influence of Step Rate on Shin Injury and Anterior Knee Pain in High School Runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc 48(7):1244-50
evidence.population: 68 high school cross-country runners
evidence.result: Lowest step-rate tertile (<=164 spm at fixed speed) had higher odds of shin injury than highest tertile (>=174 spm): OR 6.67 (95% CI 1.2-36.7); at self-selected speed OR 5.85 (1.1-32.1). Anterior knee pain not associated with step rate. Association only; does not test increasing step rate.

evidence.citation: Napier C, MacLean CL, Maurer J, Taunton JE, Hunt MA 2019. Kinematic Correlates of Kinetic Outcomes Associated With Running-Related Injury. J Appl Biomech 35(2):123-130
evidence.population: healthy novice female runners, treadmill
evidence.result: Speed, horizontal heel-to-COM distance at initial contact, foot strike angle and step length explained 37-54% of variance in impact transient, loading rates and peak braking force. Hip flexion angle and shank angle at IC did not contribute to any model.

suggestions.caveats: Moderate-certainty evidence (Doyle 2022) that step-rate retraining changes step rate and loading rate; joint-load reductions are from acute lab studies in healthy runners. Low cadence is associated with shin injury in one small prospective cohort (wide CIs); no RCT shows step-rate retraining prevents injury. Napier 2019: heel-to-COM distance, foot strike angle and step length predicted loading, but shank angle at IC did not, so shank angle alone is a weaker target. Step rate increase lowers knee flexion and knee work; effects at +5% are smaller than at +10%.

suggestions.cue: 'Run softer / quieter' with real-time feedback on impact (sound, accelerometer or force display).

evidence.citation: Chan ZYS, Zhang JH, Au IPH, An WW, Shum GLK, Ng GYF, Cheung RTH 2018. Gait Retraining for the Reduction of Injury Occurrence in Novice Distance Runners: 1-Year Follow-up of a Randomized Controlled Trial. Am J Sports Med 46(2):388-395
evidence.population: 320 novice runners
evidence.result: 2 weeks of real-time visual feedback on impact loading reduced vertical loading rates (P<.001, d>0.99). 12-month injury occurrence 16% vs 38% (control); HR 0.38 (95% CI 0.25-0.59), i.e. 62% lower injury risk.

evidence.citation: Crowell HP, Davis IS 2011. Gait retraining to reduce lower extremity loading in runners. Clin Biomech 26(1):78-83
evidence.population: 10 runners with peak tibial acceleration >8 g
evidence.result: Real-time visual feedback from a tibial accelerometer: tibial acceleration reduced ~50%, vertical loading rates ~30%, impact peak ~20%; maintained at 1 month.

suggestions.caveats: Targets impact loading rather than overstride per se. Chan 2018 RCT used instrumented-treadmill visual feedback; whether a verbal-only 'run softer' cue gives the same result was not tested in these studies.

overstride.notes: Bramah 2018 (case-control) linked a more extended knee and dorsiflexed ankle at initial contact with injury across four injury types. No strength or mobility intervention was found that was tested for changing overstride.

suggestions.cue: If very upright and knee (patellofemoral) symptoms: small forward lean from the ankles/hips ('lean slightly forward, chest over your toes'), around 5-10 degrees more.

evidence.citation: Teng HL, Powers CM 2014. Sagittal plane trunk posture influences patellofemoral joint stress during running. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 44(10):785-92
evidence.population: 24 asymptomatic recreational runners, overground 3.4 m/s
evidence.result: Trunk flexion 7.3 (self-selected), 14.1 (flexed), 4.0 deg (extended). Peak PFJ stress lower when flexed (20.2 MPa) and higher when extended (23.1 MPa) vs self-selected (21.5 MPa). Inverse correlation trunk flexion vs PFJ stress r=-0.60.

evidence.citation: Teng HL, Powers CM 2015. Influence of trunk posture on lower extremity energetics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 47(3):625-30
evidence.population: 40 asymptomatic recreational runners
evidence.result: High trunk flexion group (10.8 deg) vs low (3.6 deg): higher hip extensor energy generation (0.12 vs 0.05 J/kg), lower knee extensor energy absorption (0.60 vs 0.74 J/kg) and generation (0.30 vs 0.34 J/kg); no ankle difference.

suggestions.caveats: Acute lab studies in asymptomatic runners; outcome is modelled PFJ stress and joint energetics, not pain or injury. More lean shifts work to the hip extensors (Teng 2015), so may be unsuitable for hamstring or proximal hamstring/gluteal tendon problems (inference, not tested).

suggestions.cue: If excessive forward lean: cue a taller posture ('run tall').

evidence.citation: Bramah C, Preece SJ, Gill N, Herrington L 2018. Is There a Pathological Gait Associated With Common Soft Tissue Running Injuries? Am J Sports Med 46(12):3023-3031
evidence.population: 72 injured runners (PFP, ITBS, MTSS, Achilles tendinopathy; n=18 each) vs 36 controls
evidence.result: Injured runners had greater contralateral pelvic drop and forward trunk lean at midstance and a more extended knee and dorsiflexed ankle at initial contact, consistent across subgroups. Each 1 deg increase in pelvic drop = 80% higher odds of being classified injured. Association, not causation.

suggestions.caveats: Only association evidence: injured runners showed greater forward trunk lean at midstance (Bramah 2018). No trial was found testing a 'run tall' cue to reduce excessive lean or injury. Teng 2014 shows a more upright trunk raises PFJ stress, so reducing lean has a knee-load trade-off.

trunk_forward_lean.notes: The two directions conflict: more lean lowers knee load and raises hip demand. Choose by symptom location.

suggestions.cue: Mirror or video feedback on treadmill: 'keep knees apart / pelvis level, don't let the knee drift inward', faded over 8 sessions.

evidence.citation: Willy RW, Scholz JP, Davis IS 2012. Mirror gait retraining for the treatment of patellofemoral pain in female runners. Clin Biomech 27(10):1045-51
evidence.population: 10 female runners with PFP and abnormal hip mechanics
evidence.result: 8 sessions of mirror plus verbal feedback on lower-limb alignment on treadmill (faded over last 4). Reduced peak hip adduction, contralateral pelvic drop and hip abduction moment during running (effect size 0.69-2.91); transfer to single-leg squat and step descent; pain and function improved; mostly maintained at 1 and 3 months.

evidence.citation: Noehren B, Scholz J, Davis I 2011. The effect of real-time gait retraining on hip kinematics, pain and function in subjects with patellofemoral pain syndrome. Br J Sports Med 45(9):691-6
evidence.population: 10 runners with PFPS
evidence.result: 8 sessions of real-time hip adduction feedback (faded). Significant reductions in hip adduction and contralateral pelvic drop while running; pain and function improved; maintained at 1 month. Instantaneous and average vertical load rates fell 18% and 20%.

evidence.citation: Neal BS, Barton CJ, Gallie R, O'Halloran P, Morrissey D 2016. Runners with patellofemoral pain have altered biomechanics which targeted interventions can modify: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Gait Posture 45:69-82
evidence.population: 28 studies in running-related PFP
evidence.result: Very limited evidence that peak hip adduction is a PFP risk factor in female runners; moderate evidence of association with hip adduction, IR, contralateral pelvic drop and reduced hip flexion. Limited evidence that both running retraining and proximal strengthening improve pain and function, but only running retraining significantly reduced peak hip adduction.

evidence.citation: Barton CJ, Bonanno DR, Carr J, Neal BS, Malliaras P, Franklyn-Miller A, Menz HB 2016. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 50(9):513-26
evidence.population: 46 biomechanical studies plus clinical studies; 16 international experts
evidence.result: Limited evidence: transition to forefoot/midfoot strike and increased step rate or altered proximal mechanics for anterior exertional lower leg pain; visual and verbal feedback to reduce hip adduction in females with PFP. Experts recommend retraining for several other conditions despite little clinical evidence.

suggestions.caveats: Two small uncontrolled studies (n=10 each) in runners with PFP showed reduced hip adduction and pelvic drop with pain/function gains up to 1-3 months. Reviews rate the clinical evidence as limited. Exact verbal cue wording was not stated in the abstracts read.

suggestions.cue: Increase step rate ~7.5-10%.

evidence.citation: Heiderscheit BC, Chumanov ES, Michalski MP, Wille CM, Ryan MB 2011. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 43(2):296-302
evidence.population: 45 healthy recreational runners, treadmill, step rate preferred, +/-5%, +/-10%
evidence.result: Less knee energy absorption at +5% and +10% step rate; less hip energy absorption at +10% only. Step length, COM vertical excursion, braking impulse and peak knee flexion decreased as step rate increased. At +10%: peak hip adduction angle and hip adduction and internal rotation moments decreased. -10% step rate increased energy absorption at all joints.

evidence.citation: Willy RW, Buchenic L, Rogacki K, Ackerman J, Schmidt A, Willson JD 2016. In-field gait retraining and mobile monitoring to address running biomechanics associated with tibial stress fracture. Scand J Med Sci Sports 26(2):197-205
evidence.population: 30 healthy runners with high impact forces (retraining vs control)
evidence.result: Cued +7.5% step rate via wireless accelerometer, 8 in-field sessions. Step rate +8.6%; instantaneous vertical load rate -17.9%; average vertical load rate -18.9%; peak hip adduction reduced 2.9 deg (SD 4.2); eccentric knee work per stance -26.9%. Changes maintained at 30 days. No injury outcome.

evidence.citation: Bramah C, Preece SJ, Gill N, Herrington L 2019. A 10% Increase in Step Rate Improves Running Kinematics and Clinical Outcomes in Runners With Patellofemoral Pain at 4 Weeks and 3 Months. Am J Sports Med 47(14):3406-3413
evidence.population: 12 runners with PFP and frontal-plane hip/pelvis kinematics >1 SD above reference
evidence.result: Single session, +10% step rate with metronome, self-monitored with GPS watch. At follow-up: peak contralateral pelvic drop reduced 3.12 deg (95% CI 1.88-4.37), hip adduction reduced 3.99 deg (2.01-5.96), knee flexion reduced 4.09 deg; weekly volume +13.78 km; longest pain-free run +6.84 km; pain (NRS) and LEFS improved; maintained at 3 months.

suggestions.caveats: Hip adduction fell about 3-4 degrees (Willy 2016 RCT, healthy high-impact runners; Bramah 2019 uncontrolled case series in PFP). Heiderscheit found the hip adduction change at +10%, not +5%.

suggestions.cue: Hip abductor / external rotator strengthening (for strength and symptoms, but do not expect it alone to change running hip adduction).

evidence.citation: Willy RW, Davis IS 2011. The effect of a hip-strengthening program on mechanics during running and during a single-leg squat. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 41(9):625-32
evidence.population: 20 healthy females with excessive hip adduction during running
evidence.result: 6 weeks hip abductor/ER strengthening plus single-leg-squat movement training: strength increased (P<.005) but NO significant change in hip or knee mechanics during running; single-leg squat hip adduction, IR and pelvic drop improved.

evidence.citation: Snyder KR, Earl JE, O'Connor KM, Ebersole KT 2009. Resistance training is accompanied by increases in hip strength and changes in lower extremity biomechanics during running. Clin Biomech 24(1):26-34
evidence.population: 15 healthy women
evidence.result: 6-week closed-chain hip rotation strengthening: hip abduction strength +13%, ER +23%. Rearfoot eversion ROM decreased; hip adduction ROM increased (P=0.05); knee abduction moment -10%, rearfoot inversion moment -57%. Did not reduce hip adduction.

evidence.citation: Neal BS, Barton CJ, Gallie R, O'Halloran P, Morrissey D 2016. Runners with patellofemoral pain have altered biomechanics which targeted interventions can modify: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Gait Posture 45:69-82
evidence.population: 28 studies in running-related PFP
evidence.result: Very limited evidence that peak hip adduction is a PFP risk factor in female runners; moderate evidence of association with hip adduction, IR, contralateral pelvic drop and reduced hip flexion. Limited evidence that both running retraining and proximal strengthening improve pain and function, but only running retraining significantly reduced peak hip adduction.

suggestions.caveats: Willy & Davis 2011 RCT: strength increased but running mechanics did not change. Snyder 2009: hip adduction ROM actually increased. Neal 2016: strengthening improved pain/function but only retraining reduced hip adduction.

hip_adduction.notes: Prospective cohorts (female runners) link greater hip adduction to later PFP (Noehren 2013) and ITBS (Noehren 2007). These are the basis for treating it as a flag.

risk_evidence.citation: Noehren B, Hamill J, Davis I 2013. Prospective evidence for a hip etiology in patellofemoral pain. Med Sci Sports Exerc 45(6):1120-4
risk_evidence.population: 400 healthy female runners followed 2 years; 15 PFP cases vs 15 controls
risk_evidence.result: Runners who developed PFP had greater hip adduction at baseline (P=0.007); hip IR and rearfoot eversion not different.

risk_evidence.citation: Noehren B, Davis I, Hamill J 2007. ASB clinical biomechanics award winner 2006 prospective study of the biomechanical factors associated with iliotibial band syndrome. Clin Biomech 22(9):951-6
risk_evidence.population: female recreational runners followed 2 years; 18 ITBS cases vs matched controls
risk_evidence.result: Runners who developed ITBS had greater peak hip adduction and knee internal rotation; rearfoot eversion, knee flexion and joint moments not different.

suggestions.cue: Increase step rate 10% (metronome), self-monitored with a watch.

evidence.citation: Bramah C, Preece SJ, Gill N, Herrington L 2019. A 10% Increase in Step Rate Improves Running Kinematics and Clinical Outcomes in Runners With Patellofemoral Pain at 4 Weeks and 3 Months. Am J Sports Med 47(14):3406-3413
evidence.population: 12 runners with PFP and frontal-plane hip/pelvis kinematics >1 SD above reference
evidence.result: Single session, +10% step rate with metronome, self-monitored with GPS watch. At follow-up: peak contralateral pelvic drop reduced 3.12 deg (95% CI 1.88-4.37), hip adduction reduced 3.99 deg (2.01-5.96), knee flexion reduced 4.09 deg; weekly volume +13.78 km; longest pain-free run +6.84 km; pain (NRS) and LEFS improved; maintained at 3 months.

suggestions.caveats: Single uncontrolled case series (n=12) in PFP runners selected for abnormal frontal-plane kinematics; pelvic drop fell about 3 degrees with pain/function gains at 3 months.

suggestions.cue: Mirror or real-time feedback: 'keep your pelvis level'.

evidence.citation: Willy RW, Scholz JP, Davis IS 2012. Mirror gait retraining for the treatment of patellofemoral pain in female runners. Clin Biomech 27(10):1045-51
evidence.population: 10 female runners with PFP and abnormal hip mechanics
evidence.result: 8 sessions of mirror plus verbal feedback on lower-limb alignment on treadmill (faded over last 4). Reduced peak hip adduction, contralateral pelvic drop and hip abduction moment during running (effect size 0.69-2.91); transfer to single-leg squat and step descent; pain and function improved; mostly maintained at 1 and 3 months.

evidence.citation: Noehren B, Scholz J, Davis I 2011. The effect of real-time gait retraining on hip kinematics, pain and function in subjects with patellofemoral pain syndrome. Br J Sports Med 45(9):691-6
evidence.population: 10 runners with PFPS
evidence.result: 8 sessions of real-time hip adduction feedback (faded). Significant reductions in hip adduction and contralateral pelvic drop while running; pain and function improved; maintained at 1 month. Instantaneous and average vertical load rates fell 18% and 20%.

suggestions.caveats: Pelvic drop reduction was a secondary outcome in small uncontrolled studies in PFP.

suggestions.cue: Shorter stride.

evidence.citation: Boyer ER, Derrick TR 2015. Select injury-related variables are affected by stride length and foot strike style during running. Am J Sports Med 43(9):2310-7
evidence.population: 42 healthy runners, rearfoot and forefoot strike at preferred, -5% and -10% stride length
evidence.result: Shortening stride: pelvic drop -0.8 deg, hip adduction -1.5 deg, ITB strain/strain rate decreased slightly, step width widened. Forefoot strike: pelvic drop 0.7 deg less but step width 1.5 cm narrower than rearfoot.

suggestions.caveats: Acute lab change of under 1 degree in healthy runners; clinical meaning unclear.

suggestions.cue: Hip abductor strengthening (expect strength/symptom change, not necessarily running pelvic drop change).

evidence.citation: Willy RW, Davis IS 2011. The effect of a hip-strengthening program on mechanics during running and during a single-leg squat. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 41(9):625-32
evidence.population: 20 healthy females with excessive hip adduction during running
evidence.result: 6 weeks hip abductor/ER strengthening plus single-leg-squat movement training: strength increased (P<.005) but NO significant change in hip or knee mechanics during running; single-leg squat hip adduction, IR and pelvic drop improved.

suggestions.caveats: Pelvic drop improved only in the single-leg squat, not in running.

pelvic_drop.notes: Bramah 2018 (case-control): pelvic drop was the variable most strongly associated with injury (1 deg = 80% higher odds). 2D pelvic drop relates to 3D pelvic drop (Dingenen 2018) and differed between knee-injured and uninjured runners (Dingenen 2019).

risk_evidence.citation: Bramah C, Preece SJ, Gill N, Herrington L 2018. Is There a Pathological Gait Associated With Common Soft Tissue Running Injuries? Am J Sports Med 46(12):3023-3031
risk_evidence.population: 72 injured runners (PFP, ITBS, MTSS, Achilles tendinopathy; n=18 each) vs 36 controls
risk_evidence.result: Injured runners had greater contralateral pelvic drop and forward trunk lean at midstance and a more extended knee and dorsiflexed ankle at initial contact, consistent across subgroups. Each 1 deg increase in pelvic drop = 80% higher odds of being classified injured. Association, not causation.

risk_evidence.citation: Dingenen B, Staes FF, Santermans L, et al. 2018. Are two-dimensional measured frontal plane angles related to three-dimensional measured kinematic profiles during running? Phys Ther Sport 29:84-92
risk_evidence.result: 2D pelvic drop, femoral adduction and hip adduction related to 3D hip adduction; 2D pelvic drop related to 3D pelvic drop. 2D knee valgus was NOT related to 3D knee abduction. 2D angle reliability ICC 0.90-0.99.

risk_evidence.citation: Dingenen B, Malliaras P, Janssen T, Ceyssens L, Vanelderen R, Barton CJ 2019. Two-dimensional video analysis can discriminate differences in running kinematics between recreational runners with and without running-related knee injury. Phys Ther Sport 38:184-191
risk_evidence.population: 42 recreational runners (18 with anterior/lateral knee pain)
risk_evidence.result: Injured group had greater 2D contralateral pelvic drop (P=.035), femoral adduction (P=.021) and hip adduction (P=.001) at midstance and smaller foot inclination at IC (P=.031). Lateral trunk position not reported as different in abstract.

suggestions.cue: Treat via the hip: mirror/real-time feedback on hip adduction and step-rate increase (see hip_adduction).

evidence.citation: Willy RW, Scholz JP, Davis IS 2012. Mirror gait retraining for the treatment of patellofemoral pain in female runners. Clin Biomech 27(10):1045-51
evidence.population: 10 female runners with PFP and abnormal hip mechanics
evidence.result: 8 sessions of mirror plus verbal feedback on lower-limb alignment on treadmill (faded over last 4). Reduced peak hip adduction, contralateral pelvic drop and hip abduction moment during running (effect size 0.69-2.91); transfer to single-leg squat and step descent; pain and function improved; mostly maintained at 1 and 3 months.

evidence.citation: Noehren B, Scholz J, Davis I 2011. The effect of real-time gait retraining on hip kinematics, pain and function in subjects with patellofemoral pain syndrome. Br J Sports Med 45(9):691-6
evidence.population: 10 runners with PFPS
evidence.result: 8 sessions of real-time hip adduction feedback (faded). Significant reductions in hip adduction and contralateral pelvic drop while running; pain and function improved; maintained at 1 month. Instantaneous and average vertical load rates fell 18% and 20%.

evidence.citation: Heiderscheit BC, Chumanov ES, Michalski MP, Wille CM, Ryan MB 2011. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 43(2):296-302
evidence.population: 45 healthy recreational runners, treadmill, step rate preferred, +/-5%, +/-10%
evidence.result: Less knee energy absorption at +5% and +10% step rate; less hip energy absorption at +10% only. Step length, COM vertical excursion, braking impulse and peak knee flexion decreased as step rate increased. At +10%: peak hip adduction angle and hip adduction and internal rotation moments decreased. -10% step rate increased energy absorption at all joints.

suggestions.caveats: No trial was found that targeted 2D knee frontal plane projection angle in running directly. Evidence is for hip adduction/pelvic drop.

suggestions.cue: Switch from heel strike to forefoot strike (PFP runners), with gradual progression.

evidence.citation: Roper JL, Harding EM, Doerfler D, Dexter JG, Kravitz L, Dufek JS, Mermier CM 2016. The effects of gait retraining in runners with patellofemoral pain: A randomized trial. Clin Biomech 35:14-22
evidence.population: 16 recreational runners with PFP (8 vs 8)
evidence.result: 8 sessions over 2 weeks switching rearfoot to forefoot strike: knee pain reduced post and at 1 month (effect size 0.294); knee abduction improved (effect size 0.291); ankle flexion and ankle ROM changed.

suggestions.caveats: Small RCT (8 vs 8): knee abduction and knee pain improved to 1 month. Forefoot strike raises Achilles/plantarflexor load (Kulmala 2013).

suggestions.cue: Widen step slightly if also narrow.

evidence.citation: Brindle RA, Milner CE, Zhang S, Fitzhugh EC 2014. Changing step width alters lower extremity biomechanics during running. Gait Posture 39(1):124-8
evidence.population: 30 healthy runners, preferred/wide/narrow step width
evidence.result: Peak hip adduction, rearfoot eversion, peak knee abduction moment and knee abduction impulse decreased as step width increased from narrow to wide.

suggestions.caveats: Acute lab: wider step reduced knee abduction moment and impulse in healthy runners.

knee_valgus.notes: Important measurement caveat: Dingenen 2018 found 2D knee valgus at midstance was NOT related to 3D knee abduction, whereas 2D hip adduction and pelvic drop were. Consider reporting 2D 'knee valgus' as dynamic hip/femoral adduction rather than true knee abduction.

risk_evidence.citation: Dingenen B, Staes FF, Santermans L, et al. 2018. Are two-dimensional measured frontal plane angles related to three-dimensional measured kinematic profiles during running? Phys Ther Sport 29:84-92
risk_evidence.result: 2D pelvic drop, femoral adduction and hip adduction related to 3D hip adduction; 2D pelvic drop related to 3D pelvic drop. 2D knee valgus was NOT related to 3D knee abduction. 2D angle reliability ICC 0.90-0.99.

suggestions.cue: 'Run as if on two lines / either side of a line on the treadmill', i.e. widen step slightly so feet do not cross the midline.

evidence.citation: Meardon SA, Campbell S, Derrick TR 2012. Step width alters iliotibial band strain during running. Sports Biomech 11(4):464-72
evidence.population: 15 healthy recreational runners, overground, step width preferred and +/-5% leg length
evidence.result: Narrow step width increased ITB strain (p<0.001) and strain rate (p=0.040); linear increase in strain and strain rate as step width decreased; wide < preferred < narrow for strain.

evidence.citation: Meardon SA, Derrick TR 2014. Effect of step width manipulation on tibial stress during running. J Biomech 47(11):2738-44
evidence.population: 15 runners, preferred step width +/-5% leg length
evidence.result: Wider step width reduced modelled compression on posterior/medial distal tibia, anterior tension and shear at all sites (shear p<0.001). Authors suggest benefit for runners with crossover style at risk of tibial stress injury.

evidence.citation: Brindle RA, Milner CE, Zhang S, Fitzhugh EC 2014. Changing step width alters lower extremity biomechanics during running. Gait Posture 39(1):124-8
evidence.population: 30 healthy runners, preferred/wide/narrow step width
evidence.result: Peak hip adduction, rearfoot eversion, peak knee abduction moment and knee abduction impulse decreased as step width increased from narrow to wide.

suggestions.caveats: All acute lab or modelling studies in healthy runners (n=15-30): wider step reduced modelled ITB strain/strain rate, tibial stress, hip adduction and knee abduction moment. No trial of step-width retraining with pain or injury outcome was found.

suggestions.cue: Increase step rate / shorten stride (step width tends to widen).

evidence.citation: Boyer ER, Derrick TR 2015. Select injury-related variables are affected by stride length and foot strike style during running. Am J Sports Med 43(9):2310-7
evidence.population: 42 healthy runners, rearfoot and forefoot strike at preferred, -5% and -10% stride length
evidence.result: Shortening stride: pelvic drop -0.8 deg, hip adduction -1.5 deg, ITB strain/strain rate decreased slightly, step width widened. Forefoot strike: pelvic drop 0.7 deg less but step width 1.5 cm narrower than rearfoot.

suggestions.caveats: Small acute changes; forefoot strike narrowed step width by 1.5 cm in the same study.

crossover_step_width.notes: Hamill 2008 (prospective) linked higher ITB strain rate with later ITBS, giving indirect support for reducing strain rate (PMID 18583001, abstract read; not listed as intervention evidence).

suggestions.cue: Hip flexor stretching will increase passive hip extension but should not be expected to change running hip extension or lumbar compensation.

evidence.citation: Mettler JH, Shapiro R, Pohl MB 2019. Effects of a Hip Flexor Stretching Program on Running Kinematics in Individuals With Limited Passive Hip Extension. J Strength Cond Res 33(12):3338-3344
evidence.population: 20 healthy subjects with limited passive hip extension
evidence.result: 3-week home hip-flexor stretching increased passive hip extension (p<0.001) but did NOT change hip extension, anterior pelvic tilt or lumbar extension during running; change in passive ROM unrelated to running kinematics.

suggestions.caveats: Small uncontrolled study, 3 weeks of static stretching; running kinematics unchanged. Negative evidence for the common assumption.

suggestions.cue: No gait-retraining cue with tested evidence for increasing late-stance hip extension was found.

evidence.citation: Schache AG, Blanch PD, Rath DA, Wrigley TV, Bennell KL 2005. Are anthropometric and kinematic parameters of the lumbo-pelvic-hip complex related to running injuries? Res Sports Med 13(2):127-47
evidence.population: 22 previously injured runners vs 19 controls, treadmill 4.0 m/s
evidence.result: No lumbo-pelvic-hip anthropometric or kinematic parameter differed between injured and control runners.

suggestions.caveats: Schache 2005 found no lumbo-pelvic-hip kinematic difference between previously injured and uninjured runners. Report as an observation, not a red flag with a proven fix.

limited_hip_extension.notes: Evidence for treating this finding is weak. Speed strongly affects hip extension; compare at matched treadmill speed.

suggestions.cue: Consider a gradual transition to midfoot/forefoot landing only when there is a clinical reason (e.g. anterior knee pain, exertional lower-leg pain); not as a default fix.

evidence.citation: Roper JL, Harding EM, Doerfler D, Dexter JG, Kravitz L, Dufek JS, Mermier CM 2016. The effects of gait retraining in runners with patellofemoral pain: A randomized trial. Clin Biomech 35:14-22
evidence.population: 16 recreational runners with PFP (8 vs 8)
evidence.result: 8 sessions over 2 weeks switching rearfoot to forefoot strike: knee pain reduced post and at 1 month (effect size 0.294); knee abduction improved (effect size 0.291); ankle flexion and ankle ROM changed.

evidence.citation: Diebal AR, Gregory R, Alitz C, Gerber JP 2012. Forefoot running improves pain and disability associated with chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Am J Sports Med 40(5):1060-7
evidence.population: 10 patients with CECS indicated for surgery
evidence.result: 6-week forefoot-strike programme: post-run anterior compartment pressure 78.4 to 38.4 mmHg; run distance 1.4 to 4.8 km; SANE 49.9 to 90.4; no patient needed surgery; gains held at 1 year.

evidence.citation: Barton CJ, Bonanno DR, Carr J, Neal BS, Malliaras P, Franklyn-Miller A, Menz HB 2016. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 50(9):513-26
evidence.population: 46 biomechanical studies plus clinical studies; 16 international experts
evidence.result: Limited evidence: transition to forefoot/midfoot strike and increased step rate or altered proximal mechanics for anterior exertional lower leg pain; visual and verbal feedback to reduce hip adduction in females with PFP. Experts recommend retraining for several other conditions despite little clinical evidence.

evidence.citation: Doyle E, Doyle TLA, Bonacci J, Fuller JT 2022. The Effectiveness of Gait Retraining on Running Kinematics, Kinetics, Performance, Pain, and Injury in Distance Runners: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 52(4):192-206
evidence.population: 19 RCTs, 673 participants
evidence.result: Moderate-certainty: step rate retraining increased step rate (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.63-1.44) and reduced average vertical loading rate (SMD -0.57, -1.05 to -0.09). Low-certainty: non-rearfoot strike retraining increased knee flexion at initial contact (SMD 0.74, 0.11-1.37), no change in running economy. Insufficient trials on pain; two trials showed reduced 1-year injury incidence.

evidence.citation: Kulmala JP, Avela J, Pasanen K, Parkkari J 2013. Forefoot strikers exhibit lower running-induced knee loading than rearfoot strikers. Med Sci Sports Exerc 45(12):2306-13
evidence.population: 19 habitual forefoot vs 19 matched rearfoot female athletes, 4 m/s
evidence.result: Forefoot strikers: lower PFJ contact force (4.3 vs 5.1 BW) and stress (11.1 vs 13.0 MPa), lower knee frontal-plane moment (1.49 vs 1.97 Nm/kg); higher plantarflexor moment (3.12 vs 2.54 Nm/kg) and Achilles tendon force (6.3 vs 5.1 BW).

suggestions.caveats: Small RCT (PFP) and case series (CECS) show symptom benefit. Doyle 2022: low-certainty evidence it increases knee flexion at IC; no economy change. Forefoot strike increases Achilles tendon and plantarflexor load (Kulmala 2013, Kernozek 2018), so caution with Achilles/calf/foot problems. Daoud 2012 injury difference is retrospective and associative.

suggestions.cue: If large foot inclination at contact is part of overstriding, address step rate first (see overstride).

evidence.citation: Napier C, MacLean CL, Maurer J, Taunton JE, Hunt MA 2019. Kinematic Correlates of Kinetic Outcomes Associated With Running-Related Injury. J Appl Biomech 35(2):123-130
evidence.population: healthy novice female runners, treadmill
evidence.result: Speed, horizontal heel-to-COM distance at initial contact, foot strike angle and step length explained 37-54% of variance in impact transient, loading rates and peak braking force. Hip flexion angle and shank angle at IC did not contribute to any model.

evidence.citation: Heiderscheit BC, Chumanov ES, Michalski MP, Wille CM, Ryan MB 2011. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 43(2):296-302
evidence.population: 45 healthy recreational runners, treadmill, step rate preferred, +/-5%, +/-10%
evidence.result: Less knee energy absorption at +5% and +10% step rate; less hip energy absorption at +10% only. Step length, COM vertical excursion, braking impulse and peak knee flexion decreased as step rate increased. At +10%: peak hip adduction angle and hip adduction and internal rotation moments decreased. -10% step rate increased energy absorption at all joints.

suggestions.caveats: Napier 2019: foot strike angle and heel-to-COM distance were predictors of loading; correlational.

rearfoot_strike.notes: Heel striking itself is common and not a proven injury cause. Daoud 2012 and Kulmala 2013 describe habitual strikers, not retrained runners.

risk_evidence.citation: Daoud AI, Geissler GJ, Wang F, Saretsky J, Daoud YA, Lieberman DE 2012. Foot strike and injury rates in endurance runners: a retrospective study. Med Sci Sports Exerc 44(7):1325-34
risk_evidence.result: Habitual rearfoot strikers had approximately twice the rate of repetitive stress injuries of forefoot strikers; traumatic injury rates not different. Authors state causation not tested.

risk_evidence.citation: Kernozek TW, Knaus A, Rademaker T, Almonroeder TG 2018. The effects of habitual foot strike patterns on Achilles tendon loading in female runners. Gait Posture 66:283-287
risk_evidence.result: Non-rearfoot strikers had greater Achilles tendon stress in mid/late and early stance without greater tendon cross-sectional area.

suggestions.cue: No evidence-based cue. If coaching, 'relaxed arms, swing forward-back' is a reasonable comfort/efficiency cue only.

evidence.citation: Arellano CJ, Kram R 2014. The metabolic cost of human running: is swinging the arms worth it? J Exp Biol 217(Pt 14):2456-61
evidence.population: healthy runners, normal vs restricted arm swing
evidence.result: Restricting arm swing raised net metabolic power by 3% (hands behind back), 9% (arms across chest) and 13% (hands on head); without arm swing, shoulder and pelvis axial rotation amplitudes increased.

evidence.citation: Koo YJ, Ogihara N, Koo S 2025. Active Arm Swing During Running Improves Rotational Stability of the Upper Body and Metabolic Energy Efficiency. Ann Biomed Eng 53(4):1003-1013
evidence.population: musculoskeletal running models (no human participants)
evidence.result: Cost of transport 5.52 (active arm swing), 5.73 (passive), 5.82 J/kg/m (fixed arms); torso longitudinal rotation lowest with active arm swing.

suggestions.caveats: These studies show arm swing (vs no arm swing) reduces metabolic cost and trunk rotation. No study was found linking arm swing that crosses the midline to injury, or testing a cue to correct it.

arm_crossover.notes: Recommend reporting as a descriptive observation, not a red flag.

suggestions.cue: No tested running cue found. Assess hip abductor strength and pelvic control; any cue ('stay tall, don't lean over the standing leg') is untested.

evidence.citation: Foch E, Reinbolt JA, Zhang S, Fitzhugh EC, Milner CE 2015. Associations between iliotibial band injury status and running biomechanics in women. Gait Posture 41(2):706-10
evidence.population: 27 female runners (current ITBS, previous ITBS, controls; 9 each)
evidence.result: Current ITBS: 1.8 (1.5) deg greater trunk ipsilateral flexion (lean toward stance limb) and 7 (6) deg less ITB flexibility vs previous ITBS and controls.

suggestions.caveats: Only a small cross-sectional study: women with current ITBS leaned about 1.8 deg more toward the stance limb. No intervention study for lateral trunk lean in running was found.

trunk_lateral_lean.notes: Association evidence only. Dingenen 2019 measured lateral trunk position in 2D but the abstract did not report it as different between injured and uninjured runners.

unverified: Napier et al. cadence-specific retraining trial: searched PubMed but no Napier cadence trial was identified; only Napier 2015 (review) and Napier 2019 (kinematic correlates) were verified.
Exact verbal cue wording used in Willy 2012 and Noehren 2011 (only 'mirror and verbal feedback on lower extremity alignment' and 'real-time hip adduction feedback' are in the abstracts).
Whether a verbal-only 'run softer' cue (without instrumented feedback) reduces injury: not verified.
Any trial of a cue to correct arm swing crossing the midline: none found.
Any trial of a cue to correct lateral trunk lean in running: none found.
Any gait-retraining trial that increases late-stance hip extension or reduces lumbar extension compensation: none found.
Full texts were not opened; numbers are from PubMed abstracts only. Step-rate RCTs published after Doyle 2022 were not searched in depth.
